tagline.text: A beginner-friendly day hike over the grassy ridges of Nasugbu

location.label: Location
location.text: Sitio Bayabasan, Brgy. Aga, Nasugbu, Batangas (KM 83 of the Tagaytay–Nasugbu Highway)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half day to a full day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱760–1,200 (day hike from Manila, solo by public transport)

children.text: Mount Talamitam is a peak of about 630 m in Nasugbu, Batangas, known as the "little sister" of Mount Batulao and a beginner-friendly day hike. You climb along open grassy ridges with few trees, and from the summit you see Nasugbu Bay and the surrounding mountains in one sweep.
Mount Talamitam rises to about

above sea level in Nasugbu, Batangas. The jump-off is Sitio Bayabasan in Barangay Aga, at KM 83 of the highway that runs from Tagaytay down to Nasugbu. It is roughly 85 km south of Manila, so if you leave before dawn you can climb and be home the same day. It is lower and usually less crowded than nearby Mount Batulao, which earned it the nickname "Batulao's little sister."

What sets this mountain apart is its grassland rather than forest. The Talamitam trees that gave the mountain its name have mostly disappeared and much of the ridge has turned to grass; one guide says about 70% of the trail has no canopy, which is why it is also called the "Bald Mountain." The upside is wide-open sky and big views all the way up, and cattle and horses grazing on the ridge are a common sight.
The hike is beginner level. Hiking sites classify it as a difficulty 3/9 "minor climb" with trail class 1–3, and describe about
3.5 km
from the trailhead to the summit with roughly 436 m of elevation gain (one guide also gives a different round-trip distance, so treat the numbers as approximate). The ascent usually takes
1.5–2.5 hours
and the descent
1–1.5 hours
. The last stretch is a steep grassy slope and the midday sun is unrelenting, so do not take it lightly.

Note that the local government requires a guide. Many older blogs say a guide is optional, but a 2026 guide reports that a "No Guide, No Hike" policy is strictly enforced. The trail crosses private grazing land, and there have been cases of hikers getting lost or damaging fences. Rules can change, so check the latest notice and register at the trailhead first. The registration point also differs by source. Most name Sitio Bayabasan, but one June 2026 guide says the jump-off is Sitio Kayrilaw and calls the Bayabasan directions outdated, and a 2022 guide mentioned a cap of 100 hikers per day. Confirm the jump-off and any daily cap with your guide or the village registration desk before you go.

The middle section is a series of rounded grassy hills that some trip reports call "Teletubbyland." There are few trees, so photos come out well but shade is scarce. Cattle and horses roam here; if one blocks the path, calmly go around it.

From the top you can see Mount Batulao, Mount Makiling, Mount Marami and the direction of Pico de Loro, and on clear days Nasugbu Bay and islands off Mindoro to the west. Batangas towns such as Balayan, Tuy, Lian and Calatagan and the Maragondon mountains of Cavite also come into view. How far you can see depends heavily on the weather.

The start of the hike goes through village lanes and woodland and crosses the Layong Bilog River. According to one guide, there is a bamboo bridge at one crossing. After rain the rocks by the river get slippery, so watch your footing.
The stretch just below the summit is a steep grassy slope of about
. Different guides exaggerate it as "nearly 60 degrees" or "like 70 degrees," but it is short, and some accounts mention a short roped section. Gloves help on wet rock.
Many hikers stop at the river after the summit to cool off. You can swim in the rock pools, and 2026 guides list the entrance fee at
(it differs by guide). Allow about
1–1.5 hours
extra for the trip from the summit to the river and back.
On weekends, temporary stalls near the summit reportedly sell cold water, soft drinks and halo-halo. They may not open on weekdays, so fill your water bottles at the trailhead.

There is a designated campsite on a wide meadow below the summit, so an overnight hike is possible. One writer who camped in May 2026 reported such strong wind that beach tents snapped. A sturdy dome tent is a must.
Linking Talamitam, Lantik and Apayang is known as the "Nasugbu Trilogy," and the full circuit is said to take about
5–7 hours
. If this is your first time, climb Talamitam alone and save the others for another day.
Board the first bus at the DLTB or BSC Nasugbu-bound terminal near LRT Buendia in Manila. The first trip usually leaves between 2 and 3 a.m.
Tell the conductor in advance that you are getting off at "KM 83, Bayabasan." If you ride to Nasugbu town you will have to backtrack about
20 km
. Take a tricycle to the trailhead and register.
Set off with your guide. You pass through village lanes, a river crossing and then the grassy ridge.
Reach the summit and enjoy the views and photos. Prepare to head down before the midday heat builds.
Start the descent. If you like, stop at Layong Bilog to swim and cool off.
Back at the trailhead, shower, have lunch and head home. Some trip reports stop for lunch in Tagaytay on the way back.
The summit is said to be hottest around
. Climbing early to avoid those hours is the key to enjoying this mountain.

items.title: Overnight camping
items.subtitle: Stars and sunrise from a meadow camp

children.text: Arrive at the trailhead, register and find a guide. The campsite fee is listed at about
per tent.
Pitch your tent at the campsite; given the strong wind, stake it down and secure all the guy lines.
Watch the sunset and night view, then have dinner. Some reports say the Milky Way is visible on clear nights.
Climb toward the summit for sunrise. Clouds can hide the sunrise.
Break camp, pack out all your trash and descend.
Camping rules can change, so check the permitted area and fees at the registration desk first.
Take a Nasugbu-bound DLTB or BSC bus from the terminals near Buendia (Gil Puyat) or EDSA Taft. The trip is described as about
2.5–4 hours
and varies with traffic.
The one-way bus fare is listed at about
, depending on the company and whether it is air-conditioned. Check the latest fare at the terminal.
Ask to be dropped at "KM 83, Bayabasan Elementary School." If you ride on to Nasugbu town you will have to come back.
Take a tricycle from KM 83 at Bayabasan to the trailhead. It is listed at about
and varies by group size and negotiation.
If you are alone, guides suggest waiting near KM 83 and joining a small group to split the guide fee.
Drive via CAVITEX and the Emilio Aguinaldo Highway to Tagaytay, then down the Tagaytay–Nasugbu Highway. Another option is to leave SLEX at the Santa Rosa exit.
Tours from Manila run by hiking groups are often posted in social-media hiking groups and frequently include transport and fees. The package varies by organizer.

The dry season from November to April (May in some sources) is the best time to climb. January to April in particular is described as having cool mornings and clear views. But because the ridge is mostly open grass, midday in March–May is intensely hot, so an early start is essential.

During the rainy season from June to October the trail is muddy and the rocks at the river are slippery. On rainy days a guide may recommend changing the route, and summit views are often hidden by cloud.
The summit is generally windy. A thin windbreaker helps when your sweat cools.

There are not many places to stay at the foot of the mountain, so most people make a day hike that starts before dawn from Manila. To stay overnight, you can use the campsite below the summit, or book a room in Tagaytay or Nasugbu town and head out the next morning. Check prices on booking sites for your dates.

Guides say there are almost no restaurants or convenience stores near the trailhead. Bring food and water before you start; small shops along the ridge and weekend stalls at the summit sell drinks and snacks. After the hike, a common plan is to head to Tagaytay for lunch and a rest. Some people continue to Mount Batulao to the north on the same day, but consider your stamina and time.
An early start is the key. Beginning the descent before the summit heat builds makes everything easier.
Carry at least
2–3 liters
of water from the trailhead. Guides say there is no spring on the upper trail.
Bring a hat, sunscreen, arm sleeves and light gloves. There is almost no shade.
Wear hiking shoes or trail runners with good grip. Sandals are not recommended.
Register at the trailhead first and follow your guide. The rule is said to be strictly enforced.
If you meet cattle, horses or dogs, keep your distance and pass slowly. Snakes are possible, so watch your footing in the lower woodland.
Carry out all of your trash. There is no trash collection on the mountain.
If you camp, bring a wind-resistant dome tent and sturdy stakes.
This is a grassland mountain with almost no shade. Midday hiking carries a high risk of heat stroke, so climb in the early morning and bring plenty of water.
The guide requirement may be strictly enforced, so do not try to climb alone; get instructions at the registration desk.
The dirt trail and the rocks at the river are slippery after rain. Adjust your plans in the rainy season.
Near the summit, lightning is dangerous. If you hear thunder, come down off the ridge.
Grazing cattle and horses can be unpredictable. Do not approach or feed them.
Fees, guide rules and camping rules can be changed by the local government and the village registration desk. Check the latest notice before you go.
Often described as Talamitam's "big brother," some accounts cover a day hike that links the two mountains. It has a long ridge and is very popular.
Neighboring peaks described as about
1 hour
from the Talamitam summit. Hiking all three is called the "Nasugbu Trilogy."
A swimming spot to visit after you come down, with rock pools. Check the entrance fee and opening hours locally.
A seaside town to the west of Talamitam. A good place to rest after the hike, but be careful not to miss your bus stop.
